These findings identify microglial activation as a response to CPB in the setting of preserved tissue oxygenation and provide preliminary evidence of an association between perioperative neuroinflammatory changes and circulating biomarkers GFAP and NfL, supporting further investigation.

title: S.T. Narasimhan (1913-1959).
Integrative Transcriptomic and Interactome Analyses Prioritize Candidate Genes for Alzheimer's Disease.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a heterogeneous neurodegenerative disorder characterized by complex molecular alterations and diverse cognitive, behavioral, and neuropsychiatric manifestations. Although transcriptomic studies have identified several pathways associated with AD, the integration of molecular signatures with disease-related phenotype annotations and pathological aging remains incompletely understood. Therefore, this study aimed to integrate transcriptomic profiling, protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis, pathological aging assessment, and curated clinical phenotype annotations to prioritize candidate molecular signatures associated with AD. Differential expression analyses and network-based approaches were applied to publicly available transcriptomic datasets derived from distinct brain regions. Candidate genes and pathways were prioritized through interactome reconstruction, functional enrichment analyses, cluster-based analyses, and independent validation in an external dataset. In addition, transcriptomic signatures were integrated with curated clinical phenotype annotations using a knowledge-based gene overlap strategy. The analysis identified molecular signatures associated with neuroinflammatory signaling, synaptic dysfunction, endocytosis, and pathological aging. Pathways related to MAPK, PI3K/Akt, NF-κB, and TGF-β1 signaling emerged as candidate dysregulated pathways in AD. Comparative analyses of physiological aging and the AD aging comparison enabled the prioritization of candidate genes potentially more closely associated with the AD condition than with aging alone, including FOS and TAB2. Independent validation reinforced the reproducibility of several prioritized genes, including GFAP, CXCR4, CCL2, HSPA1A, FCGR2A, TLR2, CD44, TLR4, FOS, TAB2, CDC42, and SH3GL2. Integration with curated clinical phenotype annotations suggested partially overlapping molecular signatures across neuropsychiatric and cognitive phenotype annotations in AD. Together, these findings demonstrate the utility of integrative bioinformatics approaches for prioritizing candidate genes, pathways, and molecular signatures associated with AD. This systems-level framework may contribute to future mechanistic studies aimed at understanding the molecular heterogeneity of AD and its associated phenotypic complexity.

title: Anti-inflammatory effects of JI-017 in cellular and an LPS-induced endotoxemia model.
abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening condition characterized by dysregulated inflammatory responses and excessive cytokine production, leading to multi-organ dysfunction. Despite advances in supportive care, effective pharmacological strategies to directly modulate sepsis-associated inflammation remain limited. JI-017 is a multi-herbal formulation composed of Angelica gigas, Aconitum carmichaeli Debeaux, and Zingiber officinale Roscoe (2:1:1), previously studied for its anticancer properties. The anti-inflammatory effects of JI-017 were evaluated using an integrative approach combining in silico analysis, in vitro macrophage assays, and an in vivo lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced endotoxemia model. RAW 264.7 macrophages were used to assess nitric oxide production, cytokine expression, and inflammatory signaling pathways. In vivo effects were evaluated through survival analysis, serum cytokine measurement, and histopathological examination. JI-017 significantly reduced nitric oxide production and suppressed inflammatory cytokine and chemokine expression in LPS-stimulated RAW 264.7 macrophages. In vivo, JI-017 was associated with improved survival and attenuated systemic and hepatic inflammatory responses in an LPS-induced endotoxemia model. Under the experimental conditions examined, JI-017 did not reduce LPS-induced phosphorylation of the selected MAPK and NF-κB signaling proteins. Under the experimental conditions examined, JI-017 reduced inflammatory responses and was associated with improved survival in an acute LPS-induced endotoxemia model. These findings support further preclinical investigation of JI-017.

title: Adropin signaling pathways in metabolic and non-metabolic disorders.
abstract: Adropin is a secreted 76-amino-acid peptide encoded by the energy homeostasis-associated gene ENHO. First identified in 2008 as a nutrient-responsive signal linking macronutrient intake with energy balance and lipid metabolism, it is now recognized as a pleiotropic hormone with actions extending well beyond classical metabolic tissues. Circulating adropin is typically reduced in obesity, type 2 diabetes, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, atherosclerosis, heart failure, cognitive aging, and several fibrotic and reproductive disorders. However, diabetic kidney disease and some acute stress states show the opposite pattern. Two cell-surface partners, the orphan G-protein-coupled receptor GPR19 and the GPI-anchored neuronal protein NB-3/CNTN6, initiate overlapping but tissue-specific cascades: AMPK/ACC, PI3K/Akt/eNOS, GPR19/MAPK/PDK4, Notch1/Hes1, and TGF-β/GLI1. Through these pathways, adropin improves insulin action and mitochondrial fuel selection, increases endothelial nitric oxide bioavailability, restrains vascular remodeling, preserves blood-brain barrier integrity, and represses fibroblast activation. This review (i) separates metabolic from non-metabolic disease evidence, (ii) introduces an explicit evidence map distinguishing direct evidence, indirect evidence, and genuine controversy for every receptor and pathway, (iii) adds dedicated coverage of central feeding control, calcium-handling dysregulation in coronary disease, TGF-β/GLI1 signaling, biomarker interpretation, and translational pharmacology, and (iv) argues that progress now depends on receptor definition, assay harmonization, and delivery chemistry rather than on further disease associations. Remaining barriers include peptide instability, blood-brain-barrier delivery, non-standardized immunoassays, incomplete receptor pharmacology, and a narrow or bidirectional therapeutic window in kidney injury and tumor immunity.

title: Consensus-based perspectives on integrating IPX203 into Parkinson's disease management.
abstract: Motor fluctuations are a common and burdensome complication of Parkinson's disease (PD) when the disease progresses, largely driven by the short half-life and variable absorption of immediate-release (IR) levodopa. IPX203 is a next-generation modified-release levodopa/carbidopa formulation that delivers rapid onset and sustained plasma levodopa concentrations through IR granules and extended-release pellets. Clinical studies have shown that IPX203 increases Good ON time (ON time without dyskinesia plus ON time with non-troublesome dyskinesia, equivalent to ON time without troublesome dyskinesia), reduces OFF time and improves motor symptom control compared with IR levodopa/carbidopa. In anticipation of the introduction of IPX203 in Europe, nine PD specialists convened to develop consensus recommendations for its use in clinical practice. Through a structured process incorporating predefined statements, voting and moderated discussion, the group reached high levels of agreement (88.9% to 100%) across seven topics. These included defining motor symptoms control, identifying patients most likely to benefit from IPX203, positioning of IPX203 within the treatment pathway, practical considerations for switching to IPX203 from current regimens and recommendations for monitoring and follow-up. The experts emphasised that IPX203 should be considered for patients with motor fluctuations insufficiently controlled on optimised oral levodopa therapy, before introduction of device-aided therapies. They highlighted the need for flexible dose adjustments, comprehensive patient and neurologist education and practical tools to support conversion to IPX203. This consensus insight provides practical guidance for integrating IPX203 into routine care of PD patients with motor fluctuations, aiming to increase mobility and reduce treatment burden for patients with PD.

title: Effects of Serotonin Transporter Genotype and (Un)Predictable Maternal Separation on Affective, Cognitive, and Social Behaviors in Female Rats.
abstract: Serotonin transporter (SERT) variation is linked to depression risk after stress, conferring an increased risk to SERT-linked polymorphic region (5-HTTLPR) short-allele carriers, who show heightened sensitivity to cumulative stress and childhood maltreatment. To elucidate the neurobiological mechanisms underlying SERT × early-life adversity interactions, animal models capturing this genetic vulnerability are of translational relevance. We evaluated four maternal separation (MS) paradigms to determine how different forms of early-life stress influence adult behavior in female SERT-deficient rats, given the higher prevalence of depression in women and the limited translational value of male-only preclinical findings. We applied several behavioral tests to wildtype (SERT+/+), heterozygous (SERT+/-), and homozygous (SERT-/-) knockout females exposed to MS: predictable 3 h/day (MS180) or 6 h/day (MS360), unpredictable 3 h/day (MSU180), or unpredictable 3 h/day plus unpredictable maternal stress (MSUS180). Controls were 15-min handled. SERT-/- females exhibited higher anxiety-like responses, passive stress coping, and increased social exploration. MS180 and MS360 induced some anxiety-like behaviors, while MS360 increased hedonic responding. Females responded differently to MS depending on their SERT genotype. First, some anxious behaviors of SERT-/- females were attenuated when exposed to unpredictable MS (MSU180 and MSUS180). Second, MSU180 reduced object recognition in SERT-/- females, while enhancing it in SERT+/- females. Third, SERT+/- females exhibited less passive stress coping when exposed to MS360 than all other groups. Neither predictable nor unpredictable MS exposure increased vulnerability to depressive-related behaviors in SERT-deficient females. Variations in SERT expression may confer some beneficial effects in response to MS, depending on the specific genotype and behavioral domain evaluated.

title: Advances in monitoring the injured brain.
abstract: Multimodal neuromonitoring has emerged as a cornerstone of modern neurocritical care for traumatic brain injury (TBI). Traditional monitoring approaches based on intracranial pressure (ICP) and clinical examination alone have proven insufficient to capture the complex, heterogeneous pathophysiology that drives secondary brain injury. Over the past decade, significant advances in monitoring technology, including brain tissue oxygenation, cerebral microdialysis, continuous electroencephalography, near‑infrared spectroscopy, cerebrovascular autoregulation assessment and non‑invasive techniques have enabled clinicians to individualize treatment strategies based on real‑time physiological data. Concurrently, artificial intelligence and machine learning are transforming data integration and prognostic modelling, and non‑invasive and wearable approaches are beginning to extend brain monitoring beyond high‑resource neuro‑ICUs. This review examines recent innovations in neuromonitoring for TBI, highlighting invasive and non‑invasive modalities, their integration into multimodal platforms, and emerging technologies that promise to make precision neurocritical care a clinical reality. As we move toward the future of neurosurgery, the challenge lies not only in developing advanced monitoring tools but in interpreting them in the context of host‑specific factors and translating complex physiological signals into timely, evidence‑based interventions that improve patient outcomes.

title: Crosstalk Between the NRF2 Signaling Pathway and Heat Shock Proteins: Implications for Cellular Stress Response and Disease Therapy.
abstract: Cells are continuously exposed to oxidative and proteotoxic stress that disrupt redox balance and protein homeostasis. Two major cytoprotective systems-the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) pathway and the heat shock response (HSR) mediated by heat shock factor 1 (HSF1) and heat shock proteins (HSPs)-form an interconnected stress-adaptation network that coordinates redox defense, proteostasis, and cellular survival. Although historically viewed as largely independent pathways, accumulating evidence demonstrates extensive bidirectional and context-dependent crosstalk through transcriptional coregulation, protein-protein interactions, posttranslational mechanisms, and shared molecular hubs, including p62/SQSTM1 and the ubiquitin-proteasome system. This network integrates antioxidant defense with protein quality control, mitochondrial homeostasis, and inflammatory and metabolic signaling; however, NRF2 and HSR responses can also become functionally uncoupled under specific biochemical and metabolic conditions. This review critically examines the molecular mechanisms underlying NRF2-HSP crosstalk and its functional consequences in neurodegeneration, cancer, ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) injury, aging, and tumor immunity. Particular attention is given to the dual role of this axis: transient activation promotes cytoprotection, proteostasis, and tissue recovery, whereas chronic or constitutive activation can support tumor metabolism, immune evasion, and therapeutic resistance. In I/R injury, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress (ERS)-induced XBP1-HRD1 signaling may impose an additional constraint on NRF2 activity, highlighting an important limitation of endogenous cytoprotection. Finally, we discuss therapeutic strategies targeting NRF2, HSF1, and HSPs, emphasizing the challenges of systemic pathway modulation, the importance of pharmacodynamic biomarkers and molecular stratification, and the potential of rational combination approaches. A context-, tissue-, and cell-specific understanding of NRF2-HSP signaling will be essential for translating this complex stress-response network into precision therapeutic strategies.

title: Lactoferrin-modified MSC-derived extracellular vesicles facilitate BBB penetration and enhance gastrodin-induced neuroprotection in Parkinson's disease: involvement of mitophagy.
abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) severely impedes neuroprotective agent delivery to the brain in Parkinson's disease (PD). Although gastrodin (Gas) possesses neuroprotective properties, its efficacy is limited by poor BBB permeability. This study aimed to develop a brain-targeted extracellular vesicle (EV) delivery system for Gas and elucidate its neuroprotective mechanisms. A brain-targeted EV delivery system was developed using mesenchymal stem cell-derived EVs modified with lactoferrin (Lf). Gas was loaded into Lf-EVs via sonication to construct Lf-EVs-Gas nanocomplexes. The nanocomplexes were characterized by transmission electron microscopy, western blotting, and nano-flow cytometry. Trans-Barrier transport was evaluated using an in vitro Transwell BBB model (hCMEC/D3 cells), while therapeutic efficacy and biodistribution were assessed in an MPTP-induced PD mouse model. Lf-EVs-Gas exhibited a typical cup-shaped morphology, with a mean size of 79.08 nm and a drug loading efficiency of 47.08 ± 4.63%. Lf functionalization significantly enhanced BBB transport, achieving a brain Gas concentration of 10.34 ± 2.7 ng/g in PD mice versus undetectable levels for free Gas. The targeted system demonstrated superior brain accumulation versus non-targeted vesicles. In 6-OHDA-treated SH-SY5Y cells and MPTP-induced PD mice, the system upregulated tyrosine hydroxylase, reduced α-synuclein aggregation, inhibited neuronal apoptosis, and improved motor function. Mechanistically, these protective effects of Lf-EVs-Gas were associated with activation of PINK1-related mitophagy, as evidenced by elevated LC3-II/LC3-I ratio and increased TOMM20/LC3 colocalization. Lf-EVs-Gas enhanced the brain delivery of Gas and produced neuroprotective effects in cellular and mouse toxin-based models of PD. These effects were associated with the activation of PINK1-related mitophagy, supporting Lf-modified EVs as a promising brain-targeted delivery platform for Gas. Further studies establishing mechanistic causality, long-term safety, and efficacy in progressive PD models are warranted.

title: An engineered exosome-based platform for targeted delivery to endogenous neural stem cells and fate modulation after spinal cord injury.
abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) disrupts neural circuits, leading to persistent sensory and motor deficits. However, effective strategies to promote repair through endogenous neural stem cells (eNSCs) are still limited. In this work, we engineered exosomes with a newly identified peptide (TGP1) to achieve targeted delivery to eNSCs. These exosomes were further loaded with Apelin to stimulate eNSC activation and neuronal differentiation. Following tail-vein administration, TGP1-modified exosomes showed greater accumulation in the injured spinal cord and a 4.6-fold increase in co-localization with Nestin+/SOX2+ eNSC-enriched regions compared with unmodified exosomes. Consequently, the Apln-TGP1 group exhibited a 2.9-fold increase in eNSC proliferation (BrdU+/Nestin+), a 3.3-fold increase in newborn neurons (BrdU+/DCX+), and a 4.9-fold increase in BrdU+/NF200+ neuronal-lineage cells compared with the SCI group. Ultimately, the dual-functional treatment was associated with significant improvements in locomotor performance after SCI. Transcriptomic analysis and protein validation indicated that these treatment responses were accompanied by coordinated Apelin-APJ- and PPARγ-related signaling changes. Together, these findings establish a targeted exosomal strategy for modulation of eNSCs and highlight its potential for promoting endogenous repair following SCI.

title: The EULAR points to consider regarding the development of criteria for the assessment of the disease activity in adult-onset Still's disease.
abstract: This study aims to formulate European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) points to consider (PtCs) regarding the development of criteria for the assessment of the disease activity in adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD). The Task Force consisted of 23 members from 7 different European countries. A systematic literature review and a 3-round Delphi exercise involving European Experts were conducted to support the formulation of overarching principles and PtCs. Based on retrieved evidence and Experts' opinions, results of Delphi Rounds, and discussions, 3 overarching principles and 11 PtCs were developed. The Task Force agreed on the importance of an appropriate definition for the disease activity in AOSD to be valid, reliable, and easily transferable in a clinical setting. The development of specific criteria for the assessment of disease activity should include a precise definition of the clinical features that could better describe the patient condition. A clear definition of disease activity would help clinicians to adjust therapy and to identify refractory patients. A validated assessment of the disease activity is important to establish specifically designed and powered studies for comprehensive management of patients with AOSD. A uniform and reproducible definition of remission may facilitate the inclusion of a new therapeutic target into daily practice and clinical trials. The EULAR PtCs were produced regarding the development of criteria for the assessment of the disease activity in AOSD, to provide the basis for a clinical tool to be readily, reliably, and easily applied in clinical settings in order to improve patient management.

title: The association between albuminuria and coronary atherosclerotic burden in the general population.
abstract: Albuminuria predicts cardiovascular events, but its association with prevalent subclinical coronary atherosclerosis is less well defined. We examined the cross-sectional relationship between urinary albumin-creatinine ratio (UACR) and coronary atherosclerotic burden in middle-aged adults from Sweden nationwide. UACR was measured in fasting spot urine in 9424 SCAPIS participants from Uppsala and Malmö. Coronary atherosclerosis was quantified by coronary artery calcium score (CACS; n = 9277) and coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA; n = 9187) for stenosis. Linear regression related log(UACR) to log(CACS) with sequential adjustment: Model 1 (age, sex, ethnicity, site), Model 2 (+blood pressure, antihypertensive treatment, diabetes and antidiabetic treatment), and Model 3 (+LDL cholesterol, lipid-lowering treatment, smoking status, and eGFR). Logistic regression examined prevalent calcification (CACS>0) and stenosis; subgroup analyses excluded CKD, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, and diabetes stepwise. Higher UACR was associated with higher CACS in the full cohort: β = 0.21 (95% CI 0.14-0.27), 0.08 (0.01-0.15), and 0.07 (0.00-0.14) in Models 1-3, respectively. Associations persisted after excluding CKD and cardiovascular disease (n = 8448): β = 0.20 (0.13-0.27), 0.19 (0.12-0.26), and 0.07 (0.00-0.15). With further exclusions, Model 3 estimates attenuated and were non-significant (no CKD/cardiovascular disease/hypertension: β = 0.06 [-0.02 to 0.14]; additionally no diabetes: β = 0.05 [-0.03 to 0.14]). In Model 1, each log-increase in UACR was associated with higher odds of CACS>0 (OR 1.08, 95% CI 1.05-1.12) and stenosis (OR 1.04, 95% CI 1.01-1.08), but associations attenuated and were non-significant in Models 2-3. Albuminuria is associated with greater coronary calcification burden, including in broadly healthy individuals, supporting the concept that albuminuria may reflect vascular disease early in the cardiovascular disease continuum.

title: Phytocannabinoid-drug interactions: pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic mechanisms, clinical relevance and toxicological considerations.
abstract: The therapeutic use of phytocannabinoids has expanded considerably over the past decade because of their potential application across a wide range of clinical conditions. However, their concomitant use with conventional medications raises important concerns regarding drug interactions and patient safety. This narrative review provides a critical overview of current evidence on the pharmacokinetic (PK), pharmacodynamic, and toxicological interactions of major phytocannabinoids, with particular emphasis on cannabidiol (CBD) and Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), while also discussing emerging evidence related to minor phytocannabinoids and the potential contribution of terpenes. Phytocannabinoids modulate the activity of drug-metabolizing enzymes, particularly cytochrome P450 isoenzymes, and may affect selected drug transporters, thereby altering the systemic exposure and clinical effects of co-administered medications. Conversely, conventional medications that inhibit or induce cannabinoid-metabolizing enzymes may modify phytocannabinoid exposure, efficacy, and tolerability. Documented or potentially clinically relevant interactions have been reported for antiseizure medications, anticoagulants, antidepressants, opioids, alcohol, and other central nervous system depressants. However, the strength of the supporting evidence varies considerably, ranging from in vitro predictions and case reports to controlled PK and clinical studies. The magnitude and clinical relevance of these interactions are influenced by multiple factors, including cannabinoids formulation, dose, route of administration, treatment duration, pharmacogenetic variability, patient-specific characteristics, and polypharmacy. Particular attention should be given to vulnerable populations, such as pregnant women, children, older adults, and patients with hepatic impairment, in whom altered PK and increased susceptibility to adverse effects may further complicate treatment. Although substantial progress has been made in understanding cannabinoid pharmacology, important knowledge gaps remain regarding the clinical significance of many predicted interactions, the interaction profiles of minor phytocannabinoids, full-spectrum preparations, and terpenes and the long-term safety of cannabinoid-based therapies. Careful differentiation between mechanistically plausible and clinically demonstrated interactions, together with consideration of cannabinoid composition, dose, route of administration, patient vulnerability, and concomitant medications, can support safer and more individualized clinical management while guiding future research priorities.

title: The Eye-Brain Axis in High Myopia: From Retinal Deformation to Cortical Network Reorganization.
abstract: High myopia is a major cause of irreversible visual impairment and is increasingly recognized as a condition involving interactions between ocular remodeling and central neural systems. This scoping review synthesizes current evidence on structural, functional, genetic, and regulatory links between the eye and brain in high myopia. We systematically searched PubMed and Web of Science from database inception to August 2026, identifying 54 eligible primary studies. The available evidence indicates that high myopia is associated with retinal and optic nerve abnormalities, altered white matter microstructure, occipital cortical changes, and functional reorganization across visual and higher-order brain networks. However, most neuroimaging evidence is cross-sectional, and Mendelian randomization analyses have not provided evidence for a clear causal effect of myopia on brain volumes. Genetic studies suggest modest overlap between refractive error and cognitive traits, whereas educational exposure appears to contribute causally to myopic refractive development. Experimental and observational evidence also supports reciprocal regulation of ocular growth through circadian, dopaminergic, autonomic, and behavioral pathways, although several proposed mechanisms remain incompletely established in humans. Overall, the eye-brain axis provides a useful integrative framework for understanding high myopia, but longitudinal and interventional studies are required to determine causal relationships and evaluate whether neural or behavioral targets can improve clinical outcomes.

title: Vessel wall MRI predictors of postprocedural new ischemic brain lesions after endovascular treatment for basilar artery stenosis.
journal: Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery
abstract: Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI)-detected new ischemic brain lesions (NIBL) are common complications after endovascular treatment (EVT) for basilar artery stenosis (BAS), directly impacting functional outcomes in patients. This study aimed to explore the association between vulnerable plaque markers identified by high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (HR-MRI) and NIBL, and to clarify their predictive value for postprocedural ischemic events. A total of 373 patients with BAS who underwent EVT were retrospectively enrolled in this study. Patients were classified into DWI-positive (DWI+) and DWI-negative (DWI-) groups based on the presence of NIBL on DWI within 48 hours post-procedurally. Plaque burden, distribution, remodeling type, enhancement rate, and degree of stenosis were evaluated using HR-MRI. To determine independent predictors of NIBL post-procedurally, multivariable logistic regression was applied. NIBL developed in 188 patients (50.4%), with a mean age of 61.76±7.83 years, including 84 males. The DWI+ group exhibited significantly higher rates of positive remodeling (PR) (51.1% vs. 37.8%, P=0.01) and plaque enhancement (PE) (87.2% vs. 75.7%, P=0.004), as well as a greater plaque burden (13.38±40.75 vs. 6.06±29.77, P=0.033), compared to the DWI- group. Multivariate logistic regression identified PE [odds ratio (OR) =2.09, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.18-3.70, P=0.011] and PR (OR =1.77, 95% CI: 1.03-3.06, P=0.039) as independent predictors of NIBL. HR-MRI-derived vulnerable plaque markers (PE and PR) are closely associated with the occurrence of NIBL following EVT for BAS, providing imaging-based evidence for risk stratification and treatment optimization.

title: Neural correlates and sex hormonal associations of impaired feedback-learning in adolescent patients with anorexia nervosa - a longitudinal fMRI study.
abstract: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a somato-psychiatric disease that mostly begins in adolescence, involving endocrine changes including amenorrhea. It is difficult to treat as most patients have difficulties embracing change and thus, the disease often takes a chronic course. Underlying pathomechanisms including moderate neuropsychological deficits of learning and memory remain insufficiently understood. As learning and memory have been shown to be estradiol-dependent in healthy controls (HC), we conducted this assessment to investigate the impact of reduced estradiol in patients on verbal learning, memory and the underlying brain-alterations. We studied feedback-learning in 20 adolescent patients with AN at admission and following short-term weight restoration, compared to 26 age- and sex-matched HC using fMRI. Learning performance and brain alterations were compared between groups and longitudinally within the patients and their interdependence with sex hormone levels as well as clinical parameters was explored. Reduced brain activity at admission could be shown in left occipital as well as calcarine, lingual and fusiform gyrus, Ncl. caudatus and thalamus compared to HC. Following weight-restoration, activity increased along with patients' learning rate. Exploratory analyses showed brain activations to be relatively higher with shorter illness duration, its improvement was significantly greater in less starved patients. Estradiol levels were associated with learning in HC but not in patients. Feedback-learning appears deteriorated in the acute state of AN. Neural hypoactivity might make re-learning and psychotherapy more difficult thus requiring adequate renourishment first. No direct link to sex hormone-reduction in patients could be shown in this study.

title: Polytetrafluoroethylene utensils as a source of micro- and nanoplastics: Insights from a Drosophila model.
abstract: Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), widely used in household products and cookware, can release particles into food, posing potential health risks. The biological interactions of the resulting micro- and nanoplastics (MNPLs) remain poorly understood but can be clarified by linking structural and physiological effects with transcriptomic changes. Here, Drosophila was used as an in vivo model to assess size-dependent responses to PTFE micro- (MPLs) and nanoscale (NPLs) particles. Following oral exposure, PTFE-MNPLs accumulated in the midgut lumen and interacted with gut components, leading to particle erosion, fragmentation, and the release of secondary ultrafine particles. Internalised particles adhered to and damaged gut bacteria, penetrated the intestinal barrier, and compromised epithelial integrity by impairing microvilli, lysosomes, and mitochondria, ultimately entering circulation and interacting with haemocytes. Associated physiological disturbances, including oxidative stress, mitochondrial membrane depolarization, and DNA damage, were reflected in transcriptomic and RT-qPCR analyses, revealing coordinated molecular alterations underlying the observed tissue damage. Analysis also revealed extensive size- and concentration-dependent gene expression changes, with up to 2897 differentially expressed genes for NPLs and a core set of 110 genes consistently affected across treatments, highlighting the common molecular impact of PTFE-MNPL exposure. These genes were enriched in pathways governing metabolism, mitochondrial function, redox balance, immunity, neurodegeneration, apoptosis, intracellular trafficking, and cell migration. Our findings provide a comprehensive view of MNPLs' biological interactions, linking their physical properties to physiological effects across multiple levels and supported by transcriptomic analysis, particularly for the poorly studied PTFE particles.

title: The DentoNeural Axis: A Piezo channel-mediated mechanosensory pathway linking tooth loss to cognitive decline.
abstract: Two independent meta-analyses-one of 18 cohort studies (n = 356,297) and one dose-response analysis of 14 longitudinal studies (n = 34,074)-demonstrate dose-dependent associations between tooth loss and dementia. The latter reported hazard ratio (HR) 1.48 (95% CI 1.18-1.87) for cognitive impairment and HR 1.28 (95% CI 1.09-1.49) for dementia; the former reported relative risk (RR) 1.20 and 1.15 for the same outcomes. The 2024 Lancet Commission expanded modifiable dementia risk factors to 14 yet omitted oral health. The mechanism remains unknown. We propose the "DentoNeural Axis"-a Piezo2-mediated mechanosensory pathway connecting periodontal ligament to hippocampal function. Tooth loss removes pulp and periodontal innervation, while periosteal and mucosal afferents persist, potentially disrupting dual neuromodulatory pathways: (1) Piezo2+ trigeminal neurons → paraventricular nucleus (PVN) → dopaminergic signaling, and (2) Tac1 (substance P)-expressing neurons → locus coeruleus → noradrenergic signaling. Both pathways converge on hippocampus to regulate brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and synaptic plasticity. This synthesis integrates Piezo channel discovery (2010), Piezo2 immunolocalization in the human periodontal ligament (2024), and trigeminal-locus coeruleus-hippocampal pathways supported by animal models and human MRI evidence linking tooth loss to hippocampal atrophy in mild periodontitis. This hypothesis relies primarily on animal data; human mechanistic validation remains a gap. If validated, tooth preservation could join hearing aids as sensory-based dementia prevention. This model may explain the "Implant Paradox"-why dental implants, lacking Piezo2-expressing periodontal ligament, may provide incomplete neuroprotection despite restoring mastication.

title: Co-delivery of doxorubicin and quercetin with Angiopep-2 modified graphene oxide for targeted chemo-photothermal therapy of glioblastoma.
abstract: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is an aggressive brain tumor with limited treatment options due to poor drug penetration across the blood-brain barrier (BBB). As combined treatment with doxorubicin and quercetin exhibited synergistic cytotoxic effects against U87 glioblastoma cells, graphene oxide (GO) can be employed to deliver these drugs, thereby enhancing their bioavailability during chemotherapy. GO can also serve as an efficient photothermal agent under near-infrared (NIR) irradiation. In this study, we functionalize GO with the Angiopep-2 peptide ligand to prepare a GOA nanocarrier. After co-loading quercetin and doxorubicin, the GOA/Q/D nanoplatform can enable BBB crossing/tumor targeting, pH-responsive drug delivery, and efficient NIR-mediated photothermal conversion for targeted chemo-photothermal therapy of GBM. Physicochemical characterization confirmed successful nanoparticle fabrication, favorable stability, and efficient drug loading and controlled drug release. Confocal microscopy and flow cytometry analyses indicate enhanced cellular uptake of GOA by U87 cells and intracellular doxorubicin accumulation. The integration of synergistic chemotherapy and NIR-induced photothermal therapy with GOA/Q/D resulted in significantly increased apoptosis and tumor cell death. In vivo studies confirmed Angiopep-2-mediated brain accumulation in healthy and tumor-bearing nude mice after intravenous administration. Therapeutic evaluation further demonstrated significantly inhibited tumor growth and prolonged survival in glioma-bearing mice treated with GOA/Q/D through intravenous injection plus NIR laser irradiation at the tumor site. Collectively, the integration of targeted delivery, synergistic dual-drug chemotherapy, and photothermal activation resulted in markedly improved therapeutic efficacy, underscoring the potential of chemo-photothermal therapy for the targeted treatment of glioblastoma.

title: Neuroendocrine regulation of appetite and energy balance in metabolic disorders.
abstract: The physiological control mechanisms that govern appetite and energy balance function through neuroendocrine systems that link central nervous system functions to peripheral organ activities and hormonal distribution pathways. The hypothalamus operates as the main control center, which processes metabolic information from hormones like leptin, insulin, ghrelin, and gut-derived peptides to govern both eating and energy use. People consume food through homeostatic processes, which control appetite together with non-homeostatic processes, which include reward pathways and circadian rhythms. The body develops metabolic disorders like obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cachexia because these systems experience dysregulation. Central-peripheral communication breakdowns occur because of chronic energy surplus and inflammation, together with hormonal resistance. People establish their feeding behavior patterns through reward-related dopaminergic signaling, circadian misalignment, and sex hormone fluctuations. Researchers have discovered that neuroinflammation, genetic, epigenetic factors, and newly identified neuropeptides all contribute to the metabolic diseases that they study. Therapeutic strategies that target neuroendocrine pathways, which include GLP-1 receptor agonists, melanocortin receptor agonists, and bariatric surgery, demonstrate potential to restore appetite control and enhance metabolic health. This study explains how neuroendocrine systems control appetite and how metabolic disorders disrupt these regulatory processes while identifying new therapeutic possibilities and future research needs in metabolic neuroscience.

title: Mesopic Microperimetry Captures Extensive Macular Atrophy with Pseudodrusen-Like Appearance Progression Beyond Visual Acuity: A Longitudinal Analysis.
abstract: To quantify longitudinal changes in mesopic and scotopic retinal sensitivity (RS) and evaluate their relationship with retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) atrophy progression and foveal involvement in extensive macular atrophy with pseudodrusen-like appearance (EMAP). Retrospective longitudinal observational study. One hundred twenty-eight eyes from 66 patients with clinically confirmed EMAP followed at a tertiary inherited retinal diseases clinic. Eyes with ≥1 visit including mesopic and red scotopic microperimetry using a validated 20-stimulus grid and multimodal imaging (blue autofluorescence and spectral-domain OCT) were included. Associations between square root-transformed RPE atrophy size and functional metrics (best-corrected visual acuity [BCVA], mesopic RS [mRS], and scotopic RS [sRS]) were analyzed using mixed-effects models adjusted for age and intereye correlation. Longitudinal rates of functional and structural change were estimated in eyes with ≥2 visits. Cox proportional hazards regression evaluated predictors of foveal involvement. Structure-function relationships, yearly rates of functional decline, and predictors of foveal involvement. Among 128 eyes (median age, 59.5 years; 69.7% female), larger RPE atrophy size was significantly associated with worse BCVA, mRS, and sRS (all P < 0.001), with the strongest association observed for paramacular mRS (R2m = 0.42). Forty-five eyes contributed to longitudinal analysis (median follow-up, 20.5 months). Retinal pigment epithelium atrophy enlarged linearly at 3.7 mm2/year, while mRS declined linearly at -1.3 dB/year. Best-corrected visual acuity and sRS demonstrated logarithmic decline patterns. Among eyes without baseline foveal involvement, faster macular mRS decline was the only significant predictor of subsequent foveal involvement (hazard ratio, 0.43 [95% confidence interval, 0.20-0.96]; P = 0.04), corresponding to a 133% increased risk per 1-dB decrease. In EMAP, mRS demonstrated stronger structure-function associations with RPE atrophy and a more consistent longitudinal decline than BCVA and sRS. Decline in macular mRS independently predicted subsequent foveal involvement, supporting microperimetry as a sensitive functional endpoint for patient stratification and interventional trials.
